Subject: Post-call: streaming SLO qualification + cost/perf levers

Thanks again for the call earlier, Samira — good baseline to work from. Summary + immediate asks below.

TL;DR
- Aurora expects an interactive streaming feature for live chat agents: target 95th percentile per-token latency <= 120ms, sustained throughput ~250 tokens/sec overall, spikes up to 600 tokens/sec for short windows.
- Concurrent sessions estimate: 600 steady, burst to 2k.
- Key levers we discussed: continuous batching, KV/prefix caching, model quantization (8-bit/4-bit profiles), and targeted model variants for low-latency vs high-quality paths.

Action items I captured:
1) Aurora: share representative QPS/tokens CSV and a small trace sample (you said you'd export 24h sample) — Samira to send.
2) Redwood: sketch an SLO plan and cost delta matrix for 3 configs (low-latency, balanced, cost-optimized) — Ben + Karthik to draft.
3) Tech deep-dive: schedule a 60-min sandbox session next week to validate streaming fallback behavior (model variant + degrade-to-sync) — propose times.

Attachments: I attached a blank SLO/cost workbook and a tiny trace we can use to profile.

Notes from the call (short):
- Aurora cares about token-level latency for streaming UI; missing a single word can break UX.
- They prefer fallbacks over errors (e.g., switch to lower-context model variant or instantly reduce batch window).
- Security/procurement conversation is separate; we kept this focused on ops/perf.

Planned internal owners: Ben — cost/back-of-envelope; Karthik — quantization & runtime knobs; Marissa — runtime perf validation and test harness.

Next: Samira, can you drop the sample CSV and confirm a few weekdays/times for the sandbox?

—
Hannah Schmitt
Account Executive | Redwood Inference

Thanks Hannah — quick clarifications and I've attached the 24h sample you requested.

Clarifications:
- The 250 tokens/sec figure is our expected average for region us-east, measured as aggregate tokens generated per second across all active sessions.
- Concurrency numbers assume ~1.8 tokens per message on average for the chat UI (short prompts).
- Spikes primarily occur between 09:00–11:00 and 17:00–18:00 local time; those windows are usually short (2–10 minutes).

Streaming specifics:
- We need per-token flushes to the client roughly every 100–250ms; partial content is acceptable as long as ordering is preserved.
- If model latency exceeds the 95p target, our preference is graceful downgrade: reduce KV context length where safe, then fall back to a smaller quantized variant (same family) — avoid outright errors.

Attached files: aurora_sample_qps.csv, trace-sample-20250913.txt. Also included a small export of a representative message payload.

Good notes — I pulled the CSV Samira sent and ran a quick eyeball on tokens/sec distribution. A few quick observations for the cost matrix draft:

- Baseline (balanced): continuous batching aggressive but constrained to 60ms max batch delay; KV caching for repeated prefixes (20–30% hit expected from sample). Use model variant M-medium (mixed FP16 quant at 8-bit activations).
- Low-latency option: batch windows tightened to 15–25ms with dynamic small-batch fast-path kernels; fallback model M-small-llamav2-6B-4bit. Expect ~1.8x cost relative to baseline but hit <120ms 95p.
- Cost-optimized: longer batch windows (up to 150ms), strong caching, aggressive quant (4-bit) + sequence-length truncation for low-priority prompts — expect ~0.6x baseline cost, higher latency risk.

I'll assemble a spreadsheet showing expected token-cost and estimated 95p latency based on our bench numbers. Karthik — could you validate the runtime tradeoffs for continuous batching vs. per-request batching for streaming? Also include notes on KV cache TTL and cold-start miss penalty.

Ben
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>

Replying with more technical detail from the runtime perspective. Notes below should be consumable for the sandbox session.

1) Continuous batching
- For streaming UIs you want continuous (micro) batching with a configurable max delay (typical 10–60ms). Tradeoff: smaller window reduces latency but hurts GPU utilization. Our fast-path kernels (tensor-core optimized) help for small-batch scenarios, but you pay more GPU-cycles per token.

2) KV / prefix caching
- Cache at the request prefix level and maintain per-session KV shards for active sessions. Expect 15–30% token reduction on our sample. Cold-miss penalty is ~20–40ms (depending on sequence length) for refilling KV on first token. TTLs should align with session idle thresholds (e.g., 2–5 min).

3) Quantization profiles and model variants
- Recommend preparing three quant profiles: Q8 (FP16 activations, 8-bit weights), Q4-std (4-bit weight-only, per-channel), Q4-fast (aggressive symmetric 4-bit with slight quality drop).
- Map variants: M-large-Q8 (quality), M-medium-Q8 (balanced), M-medium-Q4 (cost-optimized), M-small-Q4fast (fallback low-latency).
- Fallback policy: prefer reducing context length and switching to M-medium-Q4 before switching to M-small-Q4fast unless quality drop unacceptable. Keep a short hysteresis window to avoid flip-flopping.

4) Streaming ordering and resilience
- Ensure each partial token group includes sequence ids and cumulative offsets; client should reassemble in order. On transient queueing, send a short "continuation" placeholder rather than dropping.

5) Pilot plan for sandbox
- Day 1: validate micro batching latency/throughput with 1k concurrent sessions (simulate their spike profile).
- Day 2: test caching hit rates and cold-start behavior; replay trace-sample-20250913.txt.
- Day 3: measure quant profiles on quality regressions (prompt set of 50 test items they'll provide).

I'll prepare configs and a small runbook. Marissa — can you own the test harness and the perf dashboard?

—
Karthik Iyer
